cases.abstract: A long context window specifies how much text a model can accept, not how consistently it can use the evidence supplied. This study tests that distinction by moving answer-bearing information through otherwise unchanged contexts and varying the number of distractors. Multi-document question answering on 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries is paired with retrieval of random UUID key-value pairs to distinguish evidence use from exact matching. In question answering, the tested models generally favor evidence at the beginning or end over evidence in the middle; GPT-3.5-Turbo can perform worse with the correct passage among distractors than without any documents. Standard and extended-context counterparts have nearly identical positional profiles when inputs fit both windows. Yet retrieval failures are not uniform: Claude-1.3 variants perform nearly perfectly on the synthetic task. Placing the query both before and after the data brings all tested models close to perfect key-value retrieval but leaves the question-answering pattern largely unchanged. These contrasting responses show why neither a larger advertised window nor success at exact lookup establishes that a model will consistently locate and use answer evidence in the evaluated contexts.
cases.methods: The evaluation changes evidence location without changing the question, the available answer, or the distractor set within each context-length condition. Each of 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries is paired with its annotated answer paragraph and Wikipedia passages retrieved by Contriever and screened to exclude annotated answers. Moving the answer paragraph tests positional sensitivity; varying the total document count across 10, 20, and 30 tests the effect of added distractors. Closed-book and single-answer-document conditions establish reference points for stored knowledge and directly accessible evidence. A complementary lookup task uses serialized JSON objects with 75, 140, or 300 random UUID key-value pairs and 500 examples per size. Moving the queried pair isolates position in a setting with minimal linguistic content. Both tasks use greedy decoding and score whether an annotated answer or target value appears in the output, rather than requiring an exact match to the entire response.
cases.results: The question-answering controls show that evidence availability and successful evidence use are different outcomes. GPT-3.5-Turbo reaches 88.3% accuracy with only the answer-bearing document, yet its worst 20- and 30-document configurations fall below the 56.1% closed-book reference. Evidence availability alone is therefore insufficient to improve answer accuracy. The standard and 16K variants also have nearly overlapping positional curves for 10- and 20-document inputs that fit both windows, so extra capacity does not improve evidence use in these conditions. Query placement distinguishes a narrower retrieval difficulty from the question-answering failure. With 300 key-value pairs, placing the query before and after the data raises GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) from 45.6% worst-case accuracy to perfect retrieval. The same intervention offers little improvement in question answering and slightly lowers accuracy outside the first document position. Making exact lookup easier therefore does not remove the positional difficulty of answering questions from supplied evidence.
cases.notes: Retained the diagnostic priority: shared evidence with changed position tests access, and the query-placement contrast separates exact lookup from question answering. Extended-window comparisons are restricted to inputs both variants can accommodate. Accuracy means target-answer occurrence, not full-response exact match. Architecture, instruction-tuning, and retriever-reader analyses remain outside these units; proposed causal explanations are not treated as established findings.

cases.abstract: Retrieval can supply useful passages without ensuring that a response needs external evidence or that its claims are supported. Self-RAG trains a language model to express retrieval decisions and evidence judgments as reflection tokens alongside response text. A critic distilled from GPT-4 feedback supplies offline judgments of retrieval need, relevance, support, and utility; the generator then learns these judgments itself. At inference, sentence continuations generated from different passages compete under scores combining generation probability with the model's reflection probabilities. Evidence assessment therefore affects output selection without a separate inference-time critic, while retrieval thresholds and critique weights allow behavior to change without retraining. Zero-shot evaluations of 7B and 13B models span six tasks. On PopQA, Self-RAG improves over a baseline trained on the same instruction-output pairs with retrieval added only at inference. On ASQA, the 13B model exceeds retrieval-augmented ChatGPT in citation precision, 70.3 versus 65.1, but trails in citation recall, 71.3 versus 76.6. On the 7B model, increasing the support weight improves precision while lowering MAUVE fluency scores. These findings support controllable evidence-aware generation, but better attribution does not imply better coverage or fluency.
cases.methods: Self-RAG uses reflection tokens as a learned interface between evidence assessment and sentence selection. A Llama 2 critic distilled from GPT-4 annotations labels instruction-output pairs offline, inserting retrieval decisions and, when passages are used, judgments of their relevance and support for the response. Utility tokens assess the response independently of the passage. The generator learns both text and reflection tokens through next-token prediction, with retrieved passage text masked from the loss. During inference, each retrieved passage yields a candidate sentence continuation. Segment-level beam search adds weighted reflection scores to the generation probability: each critique score is normalized within its token category, allowing relevance, support, and utility to influence which continuation survives. Thus, a passage is not merely extra prompt content; its judged relationship to the response affects selection. Changing the retrieval threshold or critique weights adjusts this process without retraining or calling the critic.
cases.results: On ASQA, Self-RAG 13B improves attribution without surpassing retrieval-augmented ChatGPT across the other reported objectives. Given the same five supplied passages, it reaches citation precision of 70.3 versus 65.1, but citation recall is lower, 71.3 versus 76.6, as is str-em answer correctness, 31.7 versus 40.7. Better-supported citations therefore coexist with less complete citation coverage and lower answer correctness. The PopQA control answers a different question: Self-RAG 7B achieves 54.9% accuracy versus 48.7% for Llama2-FT, which uses the same instruction-output pairs but receives retrieved passages only at inference. This comparison supports a benefit beyond example availability, while changing retrieval-aware training and reflection together rather than isolating either. The 7B customization analysis reveals another tradeoff: increasing the support weight raises citation precision but lowers MAUVE, while reducing retrieval degrades PopQA more than PubHealth. The controls thus expose a choice of operating point: prioritizing support or reducing retrieval can carry measurable costs elsewhere.
cases.notes: Retained joint retrieval and evidence selection as the contribution, with weighted sentence ranking explaining how reflection changes generation. Main comparisons use models trained on 150,000 instruction-output pairs. The separate ablations use 50,000 pairs and 150 sampled ASQA cases; no main-table improvement is attributed to that smaller setting. Same-pair fine-tuning controls example availability but changes retrieval-aware training and reflection together. ChatGPT comparisons share ASQA passages, not training budgets. Model-predicted reflection scores are selection signals, not independent verification.
